content: Bacillus is a genus of rod-shaped, Gram-positive bacteria that belongs to the division Firmicutes. Species within this genus can be either obligate aerobes or facultative aerobes and are characterized by their ability to test positive for the enzyme catalase. Bacillus species are widely distributed in nature and include both free-living and pathogenic organisms. Under adverse environmental conditions, Bacillus cells produce oval endospores, which can remain dormant for extended periods. While these features originally defined the genus, not all species with these characteristics are closely related, and many have been reclassified into other genera. Bacillus subtilis is one of the most extensively studied prokaryotes in terms of molecular and cellular biology. Its exceptional genetic tractability and relatively large size have made it an invaluable model organism for investigating bacterial biology from multiple perspectives. Advances in fluorescence microscopy have recently provided groundbreaking insights into the dynamic structure of single-cell organisms. Research on Bacillus subtilis has been pivotal in the fields of bacterial molecular biology and cytology, serving as a model for studying differentiation, gene and protein regulation, and cell cycle events in bacteria. Two Bacillus species are of particular medical importance: Bacillus anthracis, the causative agent of anthrax, and Bacillus cereus, which is associated with foodborne illnesses resembling those caused by Staphylococcus. Another species, Bacillus thuringiensis, is a significant insect pathogen and is often used as a biological control agent against insect pests. The type species of the genus is Bacillus subtilis, which is not only a key model organism but also a notable food spoiler, causing ropiness in bread and related products. Bacillus coagulans is another species implicated in food spoilage. Bacillus can be easily isolated by placing non-sterile soil in water, shaking it, inoculating it into melted Mannitol Salt Agar, and incubating at room temperature for at least a day. Colonies typically appear large, spreading, and irregularly shaped. Microscopically, Bacillus cells appear as rods, with many containing an oval endospore at one end, causing a bulging appearance. The cell wall of Bacillus is a rigid structure that forms the first barrier between the bacterium and its environment. It also maintains cell shape and withstands the internal pressure generated by turgor. The cell wall is primarily composed of peptidoglycan, teichoic acids, and teichuronic acids. Bacillus subtilis was the first bacterium in which the role of an actin-like cytoskeleton in determining cell shape and peptidoglycan synthesis was identified. Additionally, the entire set of enzymes involved in peptidoglycan synthesis was localized in this organism. The cytoskeleton plays a critical role in the generation and maintenance of cell shape. It is important to note that while Bacillus (capitalized and italicized) refers specifically to the genus, the term bacillus can also describe any rod-shaped bacterium. In this broader sense, bacilli are found across various taxonomic groups of bacteria. Similarly, Bacilli refers to the class to which the genus Bacillus belongs, whereas bacilli (lowercase) refers to any rod-shaped bacteria. It is also worth mentioning that the term bacillus as a descriptor of cell morphology does not necessarily imply Gram-positive staining, as rod-shaped bacteria like Escherichia coli are Gram-negative.
